1114.title: Arafah and Ashura
1114.hook: two voluntary fasts that expiate sins of past years (Muslim)
1114.howItsDone: Some Sunni Muslims fast the day of Arafah when not on pilgrimage, and fast Ashura with the day before it; for Shia Muslims, Ashura is a day of mourning for Husayn, marked with gatherings, and their scholars give their own rulings on fasting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fast of Dawud: a day on, a day off. Abdullah wanted more, and was given rest.

Someone once asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about fasting on two particular days of the year. His answers are kept in Sahih Muslim, and they reach a long way. Fasting one of them, he said, wipes away the sins of the year before and the year after. Fasting the other wipes away the sins of the year before. Neither is required. Both are remembered. One sits near the start of the Islamic year, the other near its end.
screen: `A QUESTION ABOUT TWO DAYS.` → `ONE DAY, TWO YEARS.` → `NEAR THE START, NEAR THE END.`

segments.voice: First, Arafah: the ninth of Dhul Hijjah, the month of pilgrimage, the day the pilgrims stand on the plain of Arafah near Mecca, in prayer until sunset. Muslims who aren't on pilgrimage can join that day from home by fasting it; that's the fast the hadith in Muslim ties to the year before and the year after. Second, a surprise: the pilgrims themselves aren't fasting. In Sahih al-Bukhari, people at Arafah weren't sure whether the Prophet was fasting that day. Umm al-Fadl sent him a cup of milk, and he drank it in front of everyone, standing there. The standing is the pilgrim's work that day; the fast belongs to those at home. Third, Ashura, the tenth of Muharram, the first month. A report in Bukhari says that when the Prophet came to Medina, he found the Jews of the city fasting that day, and they told him it was the day God saved Musa, Moses, and his people. He fasted it and told the Muslims to fast it. A report in Muslim adds that late in his life he said, if he lived to the next year, he would fast the ninth as well. So some Sunni Muslims fast the ninth and tenth together. Fourth, Ashura carries another weight. Tradition remembers it as the day of Karbala, where Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, was killed with his family and companions. Shia communities keep Ashura above all as a day of mourning for Husayn, with gatherings, recitations and grief, and Shia scholars have their own rulings on fasting it. The same day, held two ways, each with its reasons: a people saved, and a grandson lost.

segments.voice: Choose one of the two days in your mind. If you're Muslim and you fast, picture the morning of that fast, what you'd eat before dawn, who you'd tell. If not, picture what you might do that day to remember what it holds, a pilgrim's standing, or a family's grief.

1115.title: The odd nights
1115.hook: seek the Night of Power in the odd nights of the last ten (Bukhari)
1115.howItsDone: In the last ten nights of Ramadan, Muslims who keep them spend extra hours in prayer and recitation, especially on the odd nights; some stay in the mosque for the whole ten days, and others keep the nights at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arafah and Ashura: two special fasts, one on the pilgrims' great day, one remembering Musa saved and Husayn lost.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ steps out of his house with news. He knows which night it is, the Night of Power, and he's coming to tell the people. But outside, two men are arguing. By the time the quarrel is done, the knowledge has been lifted from him. The report, from Ubadah ibn al-Samit, is in Sahih al-Bukhari, and what the Prophet says next is the surprise. Perhaps it's better for you this way. Seek it.
screen: `HE COMES OUT WITH NEWS.` → `TWO MEN ARGUING.` → `PERHAPS IT'S BETTER THIS WAY.`

segments.voice: First, the night itself. The Qur'an gives it a short surah of its own, the ninety-seventh. In Pickthall's words: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months." The surah opens by saying the Qur'an was sent down on that night, and the hadith place it in Ramadan. Second, where to look. In another report in Bukhari, the Prophet says to seek it in the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan. Not one night, then: a handful near the end of the month, each one a candidate. Third, why not just say which? The story of the quarrel answers that, at least in part. The date was about to be given and was taken away, and the Prophet didn't call it a loss. If the date were known, people might pour everything into one night and coast through the rest. Unknown, it asks for attention across several nights, and it rewards the person who keeps showing up. Some scholars have drawn that lesson; the hadith itself leaves the reason unsaid. Fourth, what people do. Aisha describes the Prophet, when the last ten began, tightening his waist-wrapper, staying up through the night, and waking his family. In some mosques the last ten nights are full: long prayers, recitation, some people staying in the mosque altogether, children asleep on the carpets at the back. Others keep the odd nights at home, quietly. Either way, the search is the practice. And one small detail from that first story: what hid the night was two men arguing. A quarrel can cost more than the people in it.
screen: `BETTER THAN A THOUSAND MONTHS.` · `THE ODD NIGHTS OF THE LAST TEN.` · `HIDDEN, SO YOU KEEP LOOKING.` · `TIGHTENING THE WAIST-WRAPPER.`

segments.voice: If you pray, choose one night this week, or mark the odd nights of the next Ramadan, and plan a few extra minutes of prayer or recitation before you sleep. If you don't, sit with the idea of a night worth staying up for, and ask what you'd want to have done with it. No grand plan: one night, a little longer awake.

1116.title: Aisha's du'a
1116.hook: O Allah, You are pardoning and love to pardon, so pardon me (Tirmidhi)
1116.howItsDone: In the last ten nights of Ramadan, some Muslims repeat Aisha's du'a many times, in Arabic, between other prayers, and some say it at other times of the year too.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the odd nights: seek it. The Night of Power is hidden somewhere in the last ten of Ramadan.

"What should I say?" That's Aisha's question, and it's a practical one. The Night of Power is hidden somewhere in the last ten of Ramadan. Suppose she happens to know which night it is. Suppose she's standing in it. Out of everything a person could ask for on a night better than a thousand months, what should she say? She puts the question to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the answer is short enough to learn in a minute.
screen: `WHAT SHOULD I SAY?` → `IF I KNEW WHICH NIGHT.` → `A SHORT ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, the source: the collection of al-Tirmidhi. Aisha asks; the Prophet tells her to say a single line. In Arabic: Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun, tuhibbul 'afwa, fa'fu 'anni. In plain English, it calls Allah the one who pardons, says He loves to pardon, and asks Him to pardon her. That's all. Second, what it leaves out. No list of wishes, no health, no wealth, no request about the future. On a night better than a thousand months, one request, and it's for pardon. Third, the word itself: 'afw, pardon. Some teachers explain it as more than forgiving, wiping a thing away so that no trace is left, the way wind wipes a track off sand. The hadith doesn't spell that out. What it does spell out is the shape of the line. It begins not with the person's need but with who Allah is, the one who pardons. Then what He loves: to pardon. Only then does it ask. Name, then love, then the request. Fourth, how people use it. In the last ten nights some Muslims repeat it again and again, on every odd night, in case this is the one, often quietly, in Arabic, between longer prayers. And it travels outside Ramadan: after a hard day, or a mistake that's still stinging. One more thing belongs to Aisha. She didn't ask what the night would bring her. She asked what she should say.

segments.voice: If you pray, say Aisha's line now, slowly, in Arabic if you know it or in your own language, and then sit with it. If you don't, notice its shape instead: who is named first, what is loved, what is asked. Then think of one thing you'd be glad to have wiped away, and just hold it.

1117.title: Fasting safely
1117.hook: the fast is not meant to harm, and health comes first
1117.howItsDone: Muslims with health conditions may consult a doctor and a scholar before Ramadan, and a person who becomes genuinely unwell while fasting breaks the fast and makes the day up later, or feeds the poor if they cannot fast at all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aisha's du'a: you love to pardon. One line, asking the one who loves to pardon for pardon.

A crowd on a road, gathered around one man. Someone is holding something over him to keep off the sun. The travelers are on a journey with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the man in the shade is fasting. Earlier we met the people the fast bends for, and the reason surah two gives: Allah wants ease for people, not hardship. What about someone who is fasting, and something starts to go wrong?
screen: `A CROWD ON THE ROAD.` → `EASE, NOT HARDSHIP.` → `WHEN SOMETHING GOES WRONG.`

segments.voice: First, that scene on the road, in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet sees the crowd and the man being shaded, and asks what's wrong. He's fasting, they say. And the Prophet says it is not righteousness to fast while traveling. The man was keeping a fast he didn't have to keep, and it had brought him to where others had to shade him. Second, a cup of water. A report in Sahih Muslim describes the Prophet on a journey in Ramadan, with people fasting and finding it hard. He calls for water, raises it so everyone can see, and drinks. The fast he breaks is his own; the point is for the people watching: you may stop. Third, a principle. A hadith in the collection of Ibn Majah says there is to be no harm and no harming. Jurists use that line as a rule of thumb: an act of worship that causes real harm has gone wrong somewhere. So when someone fasting starts to feel faint, dangerously dehydrated, or unwell in a way that threatens their health, the books of law allow the fast to be broken and the day made up later. Fourth, the quiet part: asking. People with diabetes, on medicine with strict timing, or recovering from illness may talk to a doctor before Ramadan, and to a scholar or imam. Some find a way to fast safely with changes. Some are told not to fast at all, and feed the poor instead. Neither answer is a failure. The fast is worship, and the body that keeps it is a trust; in these hadith, taking care of it is part of keeping the fast.
screen: `A MAN SHADED ON THE ROAD.` · `A CUP OF WATER, RAISED UP.` · `NO HARM, AND NO HARMING.` · `ASK A DOCTOR, ASK A SCHOLAR.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and move your attention slowly down from the top of your head: is it clear or aching, is your throat dry, how do your stomach, back and legs feel? Don't fix anything; just notice, the way you'd notice a friend's face across the table. If something has been asking for attention a while, a checkup put off, a medicine skipped, make a quiet note of it.
Fasting safely. Keeping the fast in a way that doesn't harm the body, and breaking it when it does, as the Prophet's own example shows. Today's word.

1118.title: After the fast
1118.hook: the joy at breaking the fast and the joy at meeting the Lord (Bukhari)
1118.howItsDone: Muslims break the fast at sunset, at iftar, following the Prophet's example of a date or a sip of water first, then pray the sunset prayer and eat the main meal, at home or at the mosque.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fasting safely: not meant to harm. When a fast threatens health, it may be broken and the day made up.

A single date on a small plate, and a glass of water beside it. The table is set, the food is ready, and nobody is touching anything. Everyone is waiting for the same moment: the sun going down, the call to prayer, the end of a long day without food or drink. Then it comes, and someone reaches for the date. And the room changes. Shoulders drop. Somebody laughs. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave that moment a name.
screen: `ONE DATE, ONE GLASS OF WATER.` → `EVERYONE WAITING.` → `THE ROOM CHANGES.`

segments.voice: First, the two joys. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in a hadith where the Prophet passes on words from Allah, he says the one who fasts has two joys: a joy when breaking the fast, and a joy when meeting the Lord. Notice the order. The first joy is right here, at a kitchen table, with a date in hand. It isn't treated as a lesser pleasure to be ignored. It's named, and it comes first. Second, how the fast is broken. A report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud says the Prophet broke his fast with fresh dates before praying, and if there were none, with dried dates, and if none, with a few sips of water. Small, sweet, simple: that's why the date on the plate. The same collection keeps a line he said at that moment: the thirst is gone, the veins are moist again, and the reward is fixed, if Allah wills. The body and the reward in one breath. Third, the second joy. Meeting the Lord comes later, and the tradition places it beyond this life; the hadith says nothing more to describe it. The first joy is felt at sunset. The second is waited for. Fourth, where this leaves us. Over this stretch we've followed the fast from an intention made in the heart the night before to a date held in the hand at sunset. And it ends here, not with hunger, but with joy.
screen: `TWO JOYS, IN THAT ORDER.` · `FRESH DATES, DRIED DATES, WATER.` · `THE SECOND JOY IS WAITED FOR.` · `THE FAST ENDS IN JOY.`

segments.voice: If you have something with you, a date, a piece of fruit, a glass of water, taste it now, slowly; if not, think of the next thing you'll eat and how you'll eat it. Not on your feet, not over a screen: notice the first sip, the first bite, the change in your body. That moment is the first of the two joys, so let it be enough.

1119.title: If you are able
1119.hook: Hajj is due once in a lifetime on those with health, means and safety (3:97)
1119.howItsDone: Muslims who have the health, money and safe passage go on Hajj once in their lives; some save for years, and those who cannot go keep the intention and sometimes, by their school's rules, send someone in their place.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the fast with two joys: one at the table at sunset, and one still waited for. Today, a new part: the pilgrimage.

Three times a man asks the same question, and twice the answer is silence. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has just told the people that Allah has made the pilgrimage a duty for them. The man calls out: every year, Messenger of Allah? The Prophet says nothing. The man asks again. Silence. He asks a third time. And the answer, kept in Sahih Muslim, isn't the one he expected: if I said yes, it would become a duty, and you would not be able to do it.

First, the verse. Surah three of the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "And pilgrimage to the House is a duty unto Allah for mankind, for him who can find a way thither." The House is the Kaaba in Mecca, and the duty comes with its condition already attached: for the one who can find a way. Second, the word. Istita'ah means being able, having the capacity; it's the word jurists use for that condition. The duty of Hajj isn't on everyone in general. It's on the one who is able. Third, what able means. Scholars of the schools spell it out and differ on some details, but the broad shape is health enough to make the journey, the means to pay for it without leaving one's family short, and a road safe enough to travel. A person missing one of those isn't failing a duty; for them, it isn't yet due. Fourth, how often. That's where the man's question comes in. Some readers hear the Prophet's silence as a mercy: he doesn't add to what's been asked. And the report goes on: he tells the people to leave him be as long as he leaves them be, and to do what they're commanded as far as they're able. Scholars read it this way: the duty is once in a lifetime, for those who can, and anything more is voluntary. So the condition is part of the pillar itself. For some, the way opens early. For some, it takes a lifetime of saving. For some, it never becomes possible, and they keep the intention.
screen: `FOR HIM WHO CAN FIND A WAY.` · `ISTITA'AH: BEING ABLE.` · `HEALTH, MEANS, A SAFE ROAD.` · `ONCE IN A LIFETIME.`

If not, think of one journey you've long wanted to make, one that matters to you, and notice what stands between you and it: health, money, time, safety. No need to solve it; just see it clearly.

Your line: once, if able. Hajj waits until a person can go. See you tomorrow.

1120.title: Umrah and Hajj
1120.hook: the lesser pilgrimage any time, the greater in Dhul Hijjah
1120.howItsDone: Muslims make umrah at any time of year, sometimes more than once, and make Hajj in Dhul Hijjah on its set days; some combine the two in one journey during the Hajj season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, istita'ah: once, if able. Hajj is due once in a lifetime, on the one who can find a way.

Two travel bookings to Mecca. One is for a week in early spring, the dates picked to fit a school break. The other is for a fixed handful of days in a fixed month, booked through an agency with a waiting list, and it can't be moved by a single day. Both travelers will put on white. Both will walk around the Kaaba. One is going on umrah, the other on Hajj. From the outside they can look almost the same. They aren't.
screen: `TWO BOOKINGS TO MECCA.` → `ONE MOVABLE, ONE FIXED.` → `ALMOST THE SAME, BUT NOT.`

segments.voice: First, the verse that names both. Surah two of the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "Perform the pilgrimage and the visit (to Mecca) for Allah." The pilgrimage is Hajj. The visit is umrah. Second, when. Umrah can be made at any time of the year. Hajj has its own days in its own month, Dhul Hijjah, and outside those days there is no Hajj. That's why one booking moves and the other doesn't. Third, what's inside. Umrah is short: entering the pilgrim's state, ihram; walking around the Kaaba, the tawaf; walking between the hills of Safa and Marwah; and cutting or shaving the hair. Hajj holds those rites and adds more: the standing at Arafah we met this week, the night at Muzdalifah, the days at Mina. Fourth, lesser and greater. Surah nine speaks of "the day of the Greater Pilgrimage," and some scholars read that phrase as setting Hajj beside a lesser pilgrimage, the umrah. Lesser doesn't mean worthless. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says one umrah to the next wipes away what falls between them, and an accepted Hajj has no reward but Paradise. The schools differ on how binding umrah is: the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools hold it a duty once in a life for those able; the Hanafi and Maliki schools, a strongly recommended practice. Each gives its reasons. And this week, end to end: two special fasts, a hidden night, a short line asking pardon, a fast kept safely, two joys, a door marked if able, and today, two pilgrimages, one lesser and one greater.

segments.voice: Say it to yourself slowly: umrah, any time of year, ihram, the walk around the Kaaba, the walk between two hills, the cut of the hair. Hajj, only in Dhul Hijjah: all of that, and Arafah, Muzdalifah and Mina. If you know someone who has made either journey, picture their face and think of asking them about it.
Umrah. The visit, the lesser pilgrimage to Mecca, which can be made any time of year, set beside Hajj in surah two. Today's word.
Your line: lesser and greater. Both are named for Allah in a single verse. A week, done.
